title: Die Geschichte vom fliegenden Robert
source: Heinrich Hoffmann, Der Struwwelpeter, Rütten & Loening, Frankfurt am Main, 564. Auflage — the canonical later text in modernized spelling (via Project Gutenberg #24571). Fresh Lectorium translation from the German.
about: The last poem in Der Struwwelpeter, and the strangest. Robert goes out into a storm with an umbrella, the wind takes hold of it, and boy, hat and umbrella are carried up through the clouds — no fall, no rescue, no lesson drawn, only the flat closing line that not a soul can say where the wind took him. He is the one child in the book whose end is simply unknown, which is why the poem reads as much like a flight as a warning.

sentences.t:
Wenn der Regen niederbraust,
wenn der Sturm das Feld durchsaust,
bleiben Mädchen oder Buben
hübsch daheim in ihren Stuben.
sentences.l:
When the rain down-roars,
when the storm the field through-rushes,
stay girls or boys
nicely at home in their parlors.
sentences.i:
When the rain comes roaring down,
when the storm goes tearing across the field,
girls and boys stay
properly at home in their rooms.
sentences.n: Two compound verbs of opposite kinds: »niederbrausen« (‘to roar down’) is separable, »durchsausen« (‘to rush right through’) is not — and being inseparable, it takes the field as a plain object where English needs ‘across.’ Both »wenn«-clauses hold their verbs to the end, which is why the particles stay welded on here. »hübsch« is adverbial again, ‘nicely, properly’ (as in »hübsch ordentlich und fromm«), and »Stuben« is the plural of the »Stub« the tailor once burst into. »oder« where English says ‘and’: whichever they are, they stay indoors.

sentences.t:
Robert aber dachte: Nein!
das muß draußen herrlich sein!
sentences.l:
Robert however thought: No!
that must outside splendid be!
sentences.i:
Robert, though, thought: No!
it must be glorious out there!
sentences.n: »aber« sits in second place rather than opening the sentence — German tucks ‘however’ inside. »muß« here is not obligation but inference: ‘it must be’ = ‘I’m sure it is,’ the same double life the word has in English. »herrlich« = ‘glorious, splendid.’ »muß« is the pre-reform spelling of »muss«.

sentences.t:
Und im Felde patschet er
mit dem Regenschirm umher.
sentences.l:
And in the field splashes he
with the umbrella around.
sentences.i:
And out in the field he goes splashing about
with his umbrella.
sentences.n: »umherpatschen« is separable, and its »umher« (‘about, all around’) waits at the very end of the sentence — the splashing goes on across both lines before the word that says so arrives. »patschen« is the flat slap of feet in puddles. »patschet« is the older full form of »patscht«, kept for the meter, and »im Felde« has the old dative -e. »der Regenschirm« is literally a ‘rain-screen’ — the thing that is about to carry him off.

sentences.t:
Hui, wie pfeift der Sturm und keucht,
daß der Baum sich niederbeugt!
sentences.l:
Whee, how whistles the storm and pants,
that the tree itself down-bends!
sentences.i:
Whee, how the storm whistles and gasps,
so that the tree bends right over!
sentences.n: »wie …!« opening an exclamation puts the verb straight after it, so the storm’s two verbs come before you hear what is doing them. »keuchen« is to pant, to gasp for breath — the storm is given lungs. »daß« after such a phrase means ‘so that, until,’ the consequence, with its verb at the end. »sich niederbeugen« is both reflexive and separable: the tree bends *itself* down.

sentences.t:
Seht! den Schirm erfaßt der Wind,
und der Robert fliegt geschwind
durch die Luft so hoch, so weit.
sentences.l:
See! the umbrella — seizes it the wind,
and the Robert flies swiftly
through the air so high, so far.
sentences.i:
Look! the wind catches hold of the umbrella,
and off Robert flies, swiftly,
through the air, so high, so far.
sentences.n: The endings tell you who does what: »den Schirm« is accusative and »der Wind« nominative, so the wind seizes the umbrella and not the other way about — English word order alone would say the opposite. »erfassen« = ‘to seize, take hold of.’ »geschwind« = ‘swiftly,’ the tailor’s word from the Daumenlutscher. And »der Robert« — the article before the name, which the first stanza left off.

sentences.t: Niemand hört ihn, wenn er schreit.
sentences.l: Nobody hears him, when he cries out.
sentences.n: »Niemand« again, exactly as in the Hanns: the crowd that never calls out, here become a sky with nobody in it. »schreien« is to shout or scream, not to weep. The »wenn«-clause holds its verb to the end.

sentences.t:
An die Wolken stößt er schon,
und der Hut fliegt auch davon.
sentences.l:
Against the clouds bumps he already,
and the hat flies also away.
sentences.i:
He is bumping against the clouds already,
and his hat goes flying off as well.
sentences.n: »anstoßen an« = ‘to bump or knock against,’ separable — but here the »an« is fronted with its phrase (»An die Wolken … stößt«), which is why the sentence opens with the clouds. The accusative »an die Wolken« marks motion up against them, not rest beside them. »davonfliegen« = ‘to fly off’; »auch« = ‘too’ — the hat follows the boy.

sentences.t:
Schirm und Robert fliegen dort
durch die Wolken immerfort.
sentences.l:
Umbrella and Robert fly there
through the clouds on and on.
sentences.i:
Umbrella and Robert go flying there
through the clouds, on and on.
sentences.n: »immerfort« = ‘continually, on and on’ — built on the same »fort« that keeps turning up as a particle (»fort geht die Mutter«, the fish who »lachen fort«). No articles before »Schirm und Robert«: the two of them are named like a pair of travellers.

sentences.t:
Und der Hut fliegt weit voran,
stößt zuletzt am Himmel an.
sentences.l:
And the hat flies far ahead,
bumps at last on the sky against.
sentences.i:
And the hat flies far ahead of him,
and at last knocks against the sky.
sentences.n: Here »anstoßen« comes properly apart: »stößt … an«, with the »an« stranded at the very end of the line — the same snip the tailor’s »ab« made. »voran« = ‘ahead, out in front.’ »zuletzt« = ‘at last, finally.’ The sky is a solid thing you can knock on, which is the nursery physics the poem is working in.

sentences.t:
Wo der Wind sie hingetragen,
ja, das weiß kein Mensch zu sagen.
sentences.l:
Where the wind them to-carried,
yes, that knows no person to say.
sentences.i:
Where the wind has carried them,
why, not a soul can say.
sentences.n: »hintragen« = ‘to carry off (to somewhere)’, the »hin« marking direction away from us; the helping verb »hat« is simply left out at the end of the clause, which verse does freely and written German does often enough. »kein Mensch« is the everyday emphatic ‘not a soul.’ »etwas zu sagen wissen« = ‘to be able to say.’ The book ends with the boy still up there — no punishment, no return, nothing brought back down.
